title: Mornings with Graham & Emmy
teaser: Rural landowner wants city annexation for a data center—what it means for taxes, farmland, and local power.

lines.text: Good morning and welcome to Mornings with Graham & Emmy—the Michigan Data Wire, your podcast on Michigan's data center buildout. I'm Graham.
And I'm Emmy.
It's Friday morning, September 4, and our big story today is a rural farm pushing to join a nearby city just so a data center can go up on that land.
That annexation move would pull tax revenue and decision-making away from the township and straight into city hands.
Exactly, and residents even 30 miles away could feel the ripple effects on land use and services if it goes through.
Graham, walk us through what we know so far about this specific request.
A property owner in a rural area is petitioning a nearby city to annex the land specifically to enable a data center development.
Why go through annexation instead of just working with the township?
The township likely has stricter zoning or outright resistance to large-scale industrial projects like this, while the city may offer more favorable rules or incentives.
That tracks with the pattern we've seen across the state lately.
It does. We've had multiple townships hit the brakes on data centers in the past week alone.
So who are the main players here—the landowner, the city, the township board?
The landowner is driving it for the development opportunity, the city stands to gain tax base and jobs, and the township loses both revenue and say over what happens on that ground.
How big a deal is the tax shift in practical terms for these small communities?
Data centers can bring significant property tax revenue, so moving that from township to city budgets changes who funds roads, fire protection, and schools in the area.
And what about the farmland angle—how much productive ag land are we talking about losing?
It's prime rural acreage that would switch from crops to server farms, and once it's developed that way it rarely goes back.
Water use is always the next question with these facilities.
Cooling systems can pull millions of gallons daily, and annexation might change which local rules apply to that draw.
Power demand is the other big one—what does this mean for electric bills down the road?
Any new large load like this factors into utility planning, and ratepayers across the region end up covering upgrades if capacity has to expand.
We've seen that exact issue in the utility's latest filing just yesterday.
Right—more than doubling capacity over 20 years partly to serve data center growth, with costs passed to customers.
So if this annexation succeeds, is it a green light for similar moves elsewhere?
It could set a precedent that encourages other landowners to shop around for friendlier jurisdictions.
What happens next—public hearings, votes, legal challenges?
The city will likely hold annexation proceedings, the township can weigh in or fight it, and residents will have a window to comment.
How far along is the actual data center proposal beyond the land request?
Details are still emerging, but the annexation is the key first step to unlock the build.
This feels like another chapter in the bigger statewide pushback we've been tracking.
It is—yesterday alone we saw recalls, moratoriums, and transparency fights in multiple counties.
Let's move to those quick hits, starting with the University of Michigan computing center.
Ann Arbor residents and activists are questioning whether the new facility could tie into nuclear weapons research.
What answers are they seeking on military connections and local oversight?
They want clearer disclosure on how the project might support defense programs and how the university expansion gets reviewed.
Next up, Lenox Township residents learned about data center plans through back channels.
They're demanding full transparency after worrying about noise, power strain, and lost farmland in Macomb County.
That distrust in township leadership is understandable when info comes late.
Over in Ionia, the council discussed letting data centers tap city power and land—no vote yet, but they're open to proposals.
Residents 30 miles out could see higher utility bills if new infrastructure is needed.
In Zeeland Township, the board just approved a one-year moratorium on new data centers and related power projects.
Concerns over noise, water, and tax breaks drove that pause to give time for permanent rules.
Ypsilanti extended its own moratorium to study impacts on power rates and water supply.
Washtenaw County taxpayers might end up subsidizing transmission lines later.
A township is also using a six-month power connection freeze to stall a proposed U-M and Los Alamos-linked data center.
Local governments showing they can slow hyperscale projects even after state interest appears.
Two recall efforts made news yesterday—one failed against an official tied to data center rezoning.
The other is a new drive in Mason against the mayor over similar rezoning without enough public input.
Both center on land-use changes that could open the door to large server farms in Ingham County.
On deck, are there any public meetings listeners can attend this weekend or early next week?
Nothing major on the immediate calendar from the tracker, but several townships are still working on permanent rules after recent moratoriums.
Worth keeping an eye on those agendas as they get posted.
Full sources and the live map at the Michigan Data Center Tracker. We're back tomorrow.

episode_title: Farm Annexation Push for Data Center Sparks Tax and Control Fight
